claims.text: A protocol integrating DFT-calibrated machine-learned interatomic potentials, molecular dynamics, and thermodynamic integration can determine melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys.
Low-energy crystalline configurations are representative of the equilibrium solid states of the targeted high-entropy alloys.
Short DFT calculations can provide calibration data for machine-learned interatomic potentials.
The calibrated potentials enable large-scale molecular-dynamics simulations across the solid-to-liquid transition.
Coordination environments and diffusion behavior can track atomic-scale structural reconfiguration during melting.
DFT reference data can train interatomic potentials that capture complex bonding in multielement systems.
Machine-learned potentials make molecular-dynamics simulations more computationally efficient than direct DFT simulation.
Thermodynamic integration of solid- and liquid-state MD trajectories can accurately quantify their free-energy difference.
The solid-liquid free-energy difference permits extraction of melting temperature.
The integrated calculations permit extraction of enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-state thermodynamic properties.
The method will predict melting temperatures within ±50 K of experiment.
The method will predict enthalpy, entropy, and volume change of fusion within approximately 10% of experiment.
The method will outperform conventional CALPHAD extrapolations in accuracy and computational efficiency.
The method will outperform standard DFT-only approaches in accuracy and computational efficiency.
CALPHAD extrapolations may not fully capture the compositional complexity of high-entropy alloys.
Pure DFT calculations may require prohibitive computational effort for this application.
The method is applicable to high-entropy alloys having well-characterized crystalline states and sufficient potential-training data.
The method may be less reliable for alloys with severe local ordering complexity.
The method may be less reliable for amorphous alloys involving fundamental bonding changes.
Prediction accuracy depends on the quality and transferability of the machine-learned potentials.
